title: Refactor rerank API: explicit k-selection, stable cursors, and structured match envelopes
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Clients are confused by the current reranking API semantics around top_k (is it per-batch vs per-query), cursor semantics for pagination, and the unstructured score arrays. This causes incorrect client-side result slicing, inefficient fetch patterns, and noisy regression surface for embeddings quality changes. Goal: Provide a clear, backward-compatible or migration-friendly contract that makes k-selection explicit, returns structured match envelopes (id, score, explanation, metadata), and supports stable opaque cursors for pagination with deterministic ordering. Must support both single-query and batch input shapes, keep p99 tail latency within 1.2x current, and avoid large increases in token/compute cost by reusing cached embeddings and enabling server-side top-k optimizations.
acceptance_criteria: API accepts two input shapes: single query object and batched array; server normalizes to per-query processing
top_k parameter semantics documented: top_k refers to number of final matches returned per query; server may accept per_query_top_k array for heterogeneous requests
Responses use a structured 'matches' envelope: each match contains id, normalized_score (0-1), explanation (optional string), metadata map (optional), and provisioning hints
Pagination exposed via opaque cursor string that encodes stable sort offset; next_cursor is null when complete
Migration path: old top_k and raw arrays accepted for 6 months with a 'deprecation' header, and a server flag to return legacy flat scores for compatibility
Benchmarks show <=20% median additional CPU per request and p99 latency <=1.2x baseline for typical batch sizes
E2E tests cover: per-query top_k array, cursor roundtrip, legacy compatibility header, and structured match schema validation
design_notes: Decision: normalize incoming shapes into a canonical per-query request in the router layer to keep the serving runtime unchanged
Decision: top_k will be an integer or an array of integers (per query). If array provided, length must match batch size; otherwise scalar applies to all queries
Trade-off: opaque cursor encodes model variant + sort key + offset; this avoids exposing internal sort/tie-breaking but bloats cursor size slightly
Optimization: server will compute coarse candidate set using cached embeddings and then run a final top-k selection with similarity score recalculation to ensure stability
Compatibility: temporary header X-Redwood-Rerank-Legacy to request pre-structured response for third-party integrators
implementation_plan: Spike (2d): implement router normalization and unit tests for input shapes
Core (5d): implement structured match envelope, cursor generation/validation, and per-query top_k support in rerank service
Perf tuning (3d): add candidate window heuristics, benchmark batch sizes, and tune KV cache reuse
Docs & SDK (2d): update OpenAPI spec, JS/Go SDK examples, and migration guide
Rollout (2w): opt-in rollout behind feature flag, collect telemetry, enable deprecation header after 4w
benchmarks: Local spike: 5k qps synthetic, batch=8, median latency +12%, p99 +18% before tuning (candidate window=512)
After tuning: median +7%, p99 +10% at batch=8 with candidate window=256 and caching enabled
Quality check: rerank MRR improved by 1.6% on internal query set when using normalized_score and deterministic tie-breaker
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Clients parsing old flat arrays will break. Mitigation: support legacy response shape via header for 6 months and add clear deprecation warnings
Risk: Cursor tampering could expose internal state. Mitigation: sign/nonce cursor contents and validate signature server-side
Risk: Increased latency for long result sets. Mitigation: server-side candidate pruning and early stopping heuristics
